newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech-German declaration boosts NATO, EU hopes.
newsitem.headline: Czech-German declaration boosts NATO, EU hopes.

text.p: A Czech-German declaration aiming to close the book on World War Two is likely to give Prague's ambitions to join the European Union and NATO a healthy boost.

The declaration, expected to be signed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his Czech counterpart Vaclav Klaus in January, tries to clear historical baggage from the negotiating table as both Western groupings prepare to recruit members from the East.
In the draft text, obtained by Reuters, Bonn strongly supports the Czech drive to leave the security vacuum in which it has languished since the 1989 collapse of communism.
Prague's chief negotiator Alexandr Vondra said the door had always been open for possible Czech membership of the EU.
But he nevertheless welcomed what he called the strongest expression of backing for Prague's ambitions so far from Bonn, which has the strongest voice in the EU.

"The declaration clearly declares German support for this membership, as well as for Czech membership of NATO, and this is something new," he told Reuters on Tuesday. "It has never been sounded that strongly in any statement."

"It builds a possible basis for understanding between the Czechs and the Germans in the sense that legal and political questions from the past should not in any way burden mutual relations and cannot interfere, perhaps one day, when the Czech Republic negotiates membership of the EU," he added.

The declaration, which is unlikely to be changed before the Czech and German foreign ministers initial it later this month, carries Bonn's expressions of regret for the brutal Nazi occupation of the former Czechoslovakia.
As expected, Prague expresses regret that some innocent people suffered when the country's 2.5 million Sudeten German minority was expelled immediately after World War Two.
In Germany, a statement by Fritz Wittmann, president of the wartime expellees' association BdV, on Tuesday rejected the draft declaration as "superfluous and a failure".
"A solution has not been brought closer for any of the questions which remain open in German-Czech relations," Wittmann said.
But the declaration, which took two laborious years to negotiate, looks forward as well as back.
It underlines the Czech Republic's democratic credentials, apparently ending a row triggered in May when German Finance Minister Theo Waigel questioned Prague's "European values".

Outraged Czech politicians interpreted this to mean that Waigel was threatening to bring the issue of the Sudeten Germans, many of whom live in his home state of Bavaria, into negotiations for Czech entry into the EU.

"Germany fully supports the Czech Republic to be accepted as a member of the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty in the conviction that this is in the common interest," says the draft, which Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec and his Germany's Klaus Kinkel are expected to initial on December 20.

"The Czech Republic and the Federal Republic of Germany today share common democratic values, respect for human rights, basic freedoms and norms of international law, and are devoted to the basis of a legal state and to the policy of peace," it adds.
The Czech Republic has long been tipped as a likely member of the first wave of post-communist countries joining the EU and NATO. But there have been times when Bonn seemed more interested in Poland.
Poland has already come to terms with Germany about World War Two and has a size and location which makes it strategically much more important than the Czech Republic.
The timing of the declaration, although leaked earlier than expected, is seen as helpful for the Czechs.
NATO foreign ministers are meeting in Brussels on Tuesday and Wednesday to prepare for an alliance summit expected next summer to announce which post-communist nations can join when.
Prague also hopes negotiations to join the EU will begin in early 1998.
